When the central bank cuts its policy rate, borrowers do not feel the effect at once. ______ The first link is the banks, which must lower the rates they charge on loans; they are often slow to do so, especially when they have locked in deposits at higher rates. Linking loan rates directly to an external benchmark was meant to strengthen this weak link.
options: Borrowers' instalments fall on the very day the cut is announced.
Banks, keen to attract new borrowers in a crowded market, usually pass on such cuts in full within a few days of the announcement.
The policy rate is the rate at which the central bank lends money to banks overnight.
The cut must pass along a chain to reach their instalments, and a chain moves only as fast as its slowest link.
Lower rates are meant to encourage businesses to borrow and invest, and households to spend rather than save.

steps: "The first link" presupposes a chain, and "this weak link" picks up the idea of a slowest link; only the key introduces both.
"On the very day" contradicts "do not feel the effect at once", and "within a few days" contradicts "often slow to do so".
solution.trap: The definition of the policy rate and the purpose of lower rates are both accurate, but neither sets up the chain that "The first link" refers to.

Restaurants often place one very expensive dish at the top of the menu, even though few diners order it. Next to it, dishes priced a little lower suddenly seem reasonable. Diners who would have balked at those prices on their own now order them without a second thought. ______
options: The costly dish, in other words, is the restaurant's best-selling item.
Diners, therefore, usually choose the cheapest dish on the menu.
Next to it, the other dishes seem reasonably priced.
Restaurants should therefore remove the expensive dishes that few diners order, since they only take up space on the menu.
The costly dish, in other words, earns its place on the menu not by being sold but by making other dishes sell.

steps: The paragraph shows that an expensive dish few people order makes the next-priced dishes sell; the close states that hidden purpose.
"Best-selling item" contradicts "few diners order it".
solution.trap: "Remove expensive dishes that few diners order" seems sensible on its own, but the paragraph has just shown that such a dish raises sales of other dishes.

A city troubled by rats once offered residents a reward for every rat tail they handed in. ______ Officials were puzzled, then, to find tailless rats running through the streets: people were cutting off the tails and releasing the rats to breed. The scheme meant to shrink the rat population had given people a reason to keep it large.
options: Within weeks, however, hardly any tails had been handed in.
Within weeks, officials realised that people were breeding rats in their homes simply to claim the reward.
Within weeks, tails were arriving by the thousand, and the scheme looked like a great success.
The reward was later raised, because too few people were taking part.
Most residents, however, refused to handle rats at all.

steps: "Puzzled, then" needs an expectation that the tailless rats upset; the apparent success (thousands of tails) is that expectation.
"Hardly any tails", "too few people" and "refused to handle rats" all contradict the large number of tails that people were cutting off.
solution.trap: "Officials realised that people were breeding rats" gives away the explanation too early; officials who already knew could not then be puzzled by tailless rats.

______ When steam engines in nineteenth-century Britain became more efficient, coal use rose rather than fell, because cheaper power made it worthwhile to use engines in many more industries. A similar pattern has been seen with fuel-efficient cars, which are cheaper to run and are therefore driven more. Efficiency on its own may not reduce total consumption as much as planners hope.
options: More efficient machines always reduce the total amount of fuel used.
Using a resource more efficiently does not always mean using less of it.
Fuel-efficient cars, for instance, are driven more because they cost less to run.
Planners should therefore stop trying to make machines more efficient.
Cheaper power, by contrast, led factories to run their engines less.

steps: Both examples show efficiency leading to more use, and the last line draws the caution; the opener must state the general paradox.
"Always reduce" contradicts the coal example, and "run their engines less" contradicts "use engines in many more industries".
solution.trap: The fuel-efficient cars option makes the right point, but "for instance" has no general claim before it, and it duplicates the third sentence.

In a market for second-hand cars, the seller knows far more about a car's condition than the buyer does. Unable to tell good cars from bad, buyers offer only an average price. ______ As they withdraw, the average quality of cars on sale falls, buyers lower their offers further, and the market can shrink until mostly poor cars remain. Certified inspections and warranties help by giving buyers the information they would otherwise lack.
options: Owners of poorly kept cars, who know exactly what is wrong with their vehicles, find that price too low and stop selling.
Owners of well-kept cars, knowing their vehicles are worth more, find that price too low and stop selling.
Buyers, as a result, are willing to pay more for every car on sale.
As a result, the market quickly fills with well-kept cars.
Sellers, however, are required by law to reveal every defect.

steps: "As they withdraw, the average quality… falls" requires the sellers who withdraw to be those of good cars; only the key says so.
If owners of poor cars withdrew, average quality would rise, which contradicts the next sentence.
solution.trap: The "owners of poorly kept cars" option has the right structure (a group finds the price too low and withdraws) but the wrong group, which reverses the effect on quality.

When a company asked new employees to fill in a form if they wanted to join its pension plan, fewer than half did so. When it changed the rule so that employees joined automatically unless they filled in a form to leave, almost nine in ten stayed in. The plan, the contributions and the choice itself were exactly the same in both cases. ______
options: Employees, it seems, valued the plan more once its benefits were improved.
Most employees, therefore, chose to leave the plan as soon as they could.
Filling in a form, it seems, is a small burden that most employees are happy to bear when their future is at stake.
The plan and the choice itself were exactly the same in both cases.
What changed was only the default, and that alone was enough to transform people's decisions.

steps: With everything else held equal, the only difference was which option applied if an employee did nothing; the close names that and its effect.
"Once its benefits were improved" contradicts "exactly the same in both cases", and "chose to leave" contradicts "nine in ten stayed in".
solution.trap: "Happy to bear" the burden of a form reverses the evidence: in both setups, most people did not fill in the form.

Early medical trials often gave a new medicine to one group of patients and nothing to another. ______ To guard against this, researchers began giving the second group a dummy pill that looked identical to the real one. Later they went further: neither the patients nor the doctors assessing them were told who had received which pill, so that the doctors' expectations could not colour their judgement either.
options: The doctors who assessed the patients could be trusted to judge without bias.
Patients who received nothing at all usually recovered faster than those who had been given the new medicine.
Patients who knew they were being treated often reported feeling better, whether or not the medicine itself worked.
Such trials were cheap to run and quick to finish.
To guard against this, researchers gave the second group a dummy pill.

steps: "To guard against this" needs a problem that a dummy pill would solve; the effect of merely believing one is treated is exactly that problem.
"Doctors could be trusted to judge without bias" contradicts the last sentence, where the doctors' expectations also had to be hidden.
solution.trap: "Patients who received nothing recovered faster" describes a result, but a dummy pill is no guard against it; and being cheap and quick is nothing to guard against.

______ Business magazines profile entrepreneurs who dropped out of college and built hugely successful companies, and readers conclude that leaving college is a bold path to success. What the profiles leave out are the far larger number of dropouts whose ventures failed and who are never written about. Looking only at the winners, we mistake luck and rare talent for a reliable recipe.
options: Leaving college early is, on average, the surest route to building a successful company.
Entrepreneurs who fail are written about as often as those who succeed.
What the profiles leave out are the many who failed.
Our picture of what leads to success is distorted by the fact that we hear mostly from those who succeeded.
College degrees have lost much of their value as more and more people earn them, so dropping out costs less than it once did.

steps: The paragraph argues that seeing only the winners misleads us; the opener should state that bias, which the last sentence restates.
"Surest route" is the very conclusion the paragraph rejects, and "written about as often" contradicts "never written about".
solution.trap: The degrees sentence offers a different reason to doubt college, but the paragraph's argument is about selective evidence, not the value of degrees.

Almost all the bananas sold in the world's supermarkets belong to a single variety, the Cavendish. Because the plants are grown from cuttings rather than seeds, every one of them is genetically identical. ______ A fungal disease that has spread across Asia, Africa and Latin America in recent decades now threatens the variety in exactly this way. Growers are racing to find resistant varieties before the damage becomes irreversible.
options: This uniformity makes them easy to grow and ship, but it also means that a disease able to kill one plant can kill them all.
This uniformity protects them from diseases that would destroy a mixed crop.
Bananas grown from seed, however, taste much the same as the Cavendish.
Supermarkets prefer the Cavendish because it ripens slowly and survives long voyages from the plantations without bruising.
A fungal disease has spread across three continents in recent decades.

steps: "In exactly this way" needs a weakness described just before; the key draws it from the genetic sameness: one disease can kill every plant.
"Protects them from diseases" reverses the risk that the next sentence describes.
solution.trap: The supermarket sentence is true and on topic, but it describes no weakness, so "in exactly this way" has nothing to point to.

A district's two hospitals were compared on the share of their surgical patients who died. The larger city hospital had the higher death rate, and many people concluded that it was the worse of the two. A closer study showed, however, that the city hospital received most of the district's serious cases, many referred to it by the smaller hospital. When patients of similar severity were compared, the city hospital's results were better. ______
options: The smaller hospital, it seems, was indeed the safer place for serious cases.
The city hospital, therefore, should stop accepting serious cases.
Death rates, it seems, tell us nothing at all about the quality of a hospital and should not be published or compared.
A raw comparison, it seems, can point in exactly the wrong direction when the groups being compared are not alike.
Many people concluded that the city hospital was the worse of the two.

steps: The paragraph shows a raw death rate reversing once like is compared with like; the close states that lesson about unequal groups.
"The smaller hospital was the safer place" contradicts the comparison of similar patients.
solution.trap: "Death rates tell us nothing at all" overreaches: the adjusted death rates in the paragraph were informative; only the unadjusted comparison misled.

When the cost of ingredients rises, a biscuit maker can raise the price of a packet. Customers notice price rises at once, however, and some switch to rival brands. ______ The price on the shelf stays the same, and many shoppers fail to notice the change for months. Statisticians who compile price indices compare the cost per gram rather than the price per packet, though, so such hidden increases still show up in inflation figures.
options: Many makers therefore raise the price and put more biscuits in each packet.
Shoppers, as a result, check the weight printed on every packet carefully.
Rival brands, in turn, raise their own prices to match, so that unhappy customers have nowhere cheaper left to go.
The price of each packet stays the same.
Many makers therefore choose a quieter route: they keep the price unchanged and put fewer biscuits in each packet.

steps: "The change" that shoppers fail to notice, while the price stays the same, must be a cut in quantity; the key introduces it as a response to customers noticing price rises.
Raising the price clashes with "The price on the shelf stays the same", and "check the weight carefully" contradicts "fail to notice".
solution.trap: "Rival brands raise their own prices" follows the second sentence smoothly, but then the shelf price cannot "stay the same", and there is no "change" left for shoppers to miss.

At a country fair in 1906, about eight hundred visitors guessed the weight of an ox. Many individual guesses were wildly off, yet their median was within one per cent of the true weight. ______ When people can see or hear one another's guesses before making their own, their errors begin to point the same way, and the crowd loses much of its wisdom.
options: The crowd was accurate because most of the visitors were experienced cattle farmers and butchers who judged animals for a living.
The crowd was accurate because the individual errors, made independently, pointed in different directions and cancelled out.
When people discuss their guesses first, the crowd becomes even more accurate.
Most of the guesses, in fact, were within one per cent of the true weight.
Such contests were a popular attraction at country fairs of the time.

steps: The last sentence says shared information makes errors "begin to point the same way", which only makes sense if the key has explained that independent errors point different ways and cancel.
"Even more accurate" contradicts the last sentence, and "most of the guesses… within one per cent" contradicts "wildly off".
solution.trap: "Experienced cattle farmers" offers a different explanation (expertise), which clashes with "wildly off" and leaves the last sentence's point about independence unexplained.

Some companies claim to cancel out their emissions by paying for forests to be protected or planted elsewhere. Critics point to two weaknesses in such deals. Many of the forests were never at real risk of being cut down, so paying to protect them changes little. Others may burn or be felled a few decades later, releasing the stored carbon again. ______
options: An offset, they argue, is only as good as the extra and lasting carbon savings it can prove.
Forests, they argue, store carbon permanently once they are protected.
Paying for forests, therefore, is the surest way for a company to cancel its emissions.
Critics point to two weaknesses in such deals.
Planting trees, they argue, also gives homes to wildlife and steady incomes to the villagers who look after them.

steps: The two weaknesses are that savings may not be extra and may not last; the close sums them up as the test an offset must pass.
"Store carbon permanently" contradicts the second weakness, and "surest way" contradicts the critics.
solution.trap: The wildlife sentence has "they" (the critics) praising tree planting, which neither follows from nor sums up the two weaknesses.

When a state caps the interest that lenders may charge small borrowers, the aim is to protect the poor from exploitation. Lenders, however, face high costs in serving tiny, scattered loans, and some borrowers are riskier than others. If the cap is set below what it costs to serve the riskiest borrowers, lenders simply stop lending to them. ______
options: Those borrowers, therefore, can now borrow from lenders at far lower rates.
Lenders, as a result, compete harder than ever to win the riskiest borrowers, offering them larger loans at lower rates.
Those borrowers must then turn to moneylenders, who face no cap, so the rule can harm the very people it was meant to protect.
The aim of such caps is to protect the poor from exploitation.
Caps, it follows, should be set as low as possible to protect the poor.

steps: Once lenders stop serving the riskiest borrowers, those borrowers must look elsewhere; the close follows them to costlier informal lenders and ties back to the aim in the first sentence.
"Borrow at far lower rates" and "compete harder" contradict "lenders simply stop lending to them".
solution.trap: "Set as low as possible" seems to serve the stated aim, but the paragraph has just shown that a low cap shuts the riskiest borrowers out.
